title: PLATOS: A Power and Latency-Aware Task-Oriented Scheduling Strategy for Healthcare IoT in Fog Computing
abstract: Healthcare Internet of Things (HIoT) technology is revolutionising the healthcare industry by enabling real-time data collection and analysis for personalised patient care. However, the rapid expansion of HIoT technology introduces challenges such as increased latency and higher energy consumption in fog computing environments, particularly when managing battery-operated devices. To address these issues, this work proposes a novel scheduling strategy that optimises both power consumption and latency through task-oriented scheduling for HIoT tasks. The proposed strategy, named PLATOS (Power and Latency Aware Task Oriented Scheduling), is implemented in four sequential phases. In the first phase, HIoT tasks are categorised into three groups: priority-oriented, storage-oriented, and computational-oriented. The second phase focuses on latency optimisation by identifying the fog computing resources that yield the lowest execution delay for each task category. In the third phase, power optimisation is achieved by selecting the resources that minimise energy consumption. Finally, in the decision-making phase, high-performance fog resources are allocated to high-priority tasks while the remaining tasks are scheduled based on a mapped list derived from the latency and power optimisation phases. Simulation experiments conducted in iFogSim2 demonstrate that PLATOS reduces energy consumption by 18.72% and latency by 8.65% when compared to the state-of-the-art. These improvements enhance the efficiency and responsiveness of HIoT systems and contribute to more effective patient care and proactive healthcare service delivery.

title: RoboDreamer: Anticipatory Humanoid Locomotion with Predictive State-Space Models
abstract: Humanoid locomotion requires control policies that remain stable under imperfect sensing while exploiting temporal context for consistent motion. We present RoboDreamer, a two-stage teacher--student framework that combines next-observation consistency with randomized continuous temporal masking. A teacher is first trained on clean observations, and a student is then distilled under masked recent observations, encouraging the policy to infer missing current information from history. At inference, the same masking interface is reused for implicit closed-loop action refinement and optional multi-step action chunking. Mamba is used as the temporal backbone, while matched ablations show that masking/distillation provides a substantial part of the gain and Mamba contributes additional tracking improvements with real-time latency. Experiments in IsaacLab, MuJoCo, and on a Unitree G1 demonstrate robust motion tracking under observation masking and successful real-world deployment.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) BASED PREDICTIVE ANALYSIS OF ORAL CANCER LESIONS USING DEEP LEARNING TECHNIQUES
abstract: The World Health Organisation report (2022) says that India ranks third in lip and Oral cavity cancer out of top fifteen cancers. The statistical data given by International Agency for Research on Cancer records that 100,000 incidences occur annually with high mortality rate. The histopathological test performed using tissue cells for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC) is time intense and extremely dependent on experts may lead to diagnostic deviations due to greater workload. In order to overcome the challenges, the research proposes an Artificial Intelligence model that integrates the Fuzzy Logic (ANFIS) and the deep learning algorithms. The hybrid model is analysed using the performance metrics with an accuracy of 98.75%. Earlier the diagnose and treatment reduce the mortality rate of the humans and also increases the survival rate of the patients.

title: Quantum Machine-Learning Surrogates, Entanglement-Enhanced Magnetometry and Fault-Tolerant Resource Estimates for Fusion: A Resource-Honest Roadmap
abstract: Quantum computing and quantum sensing are routinely proposed as accelerants for fusion; a serious design program should test those proposals quantitatively rather than assume them. We deliver a resource-honest map of where the quantum toolbox helps a compact spherical-tokamak breeder and its tandem-mirror burner, and where it does not, formalised as three coupled estimation problems and computed on a single GPU-HPC campaign. On the machine-learning front we build a quantum-kernel transport surrogate and measure its classifier area-under-curve (AUC) falling with encoding width — 0.817 at four qubits to 0.691 at eight — the signature of exponential kernel concentration, for which we give the variance bound and the induced shot-cost scaling; at a realistic 37-logical-qubit problem the quantum Gram evaluation is 9–11 orders of magnitude slower than its classical counterpart. On the sensing front we derive the entanglement-advantage condition from the quantum Fisher information and specify the in-cryostat magnetometry chain for the breeder centrepost (peak field 16.84 T, kept formally distinct from the burner plug at 26.49 T): an NMR/EPR probe as the absolute monitor to ≤1 ppm, a SQUID and an NV-diamond ensemble (1 pT Hz^-1/2) for the 1 mT quench precursor, with the entanglement knee located at a normalised signal ≈0.14. Every Kronos in-bore diagnostic sits below the knee, where entanglement buys only +0.00077 AUC; above it (deep error-field mapping) a Heisenberg-limited protocol carries the standard-quantum-limit sensitivity from 5.7×10^-7 to 5.7×10^-8 T at 100 probes. On the fault-tolerant front we recompute the resource ledger from first formulas — the Grover iteration count 1.62^n and the surface-code footprint 2d^2 physical qubits per logical qubit — across 50 rows with zero discrepancy, and date the single fusion-relevant near-term niche: linear Vlasov kinetics at 11–19 logical qubits around 2029±2, with nonlinear five-dimensional gyrokinetics beyond 2035 and fleet-scale Grover search never practical (1.8×10^18 iterations). Three further workloads keep the verdict resource-honest: full six-dimensional kinetic Hamiltonian simulation at ~44 logical qubits and ~19 days, fault-tolerant phase estimation of the exact REBCO/alloy ground state at ~238 logical qubits and ~10^9 Toffoli gates, and a Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd equilibrium linear solve at ~10^17 T-gates — all calibration-only. Two of the six quantum-track items are already twin-testable classically: a materials variational eigensolver reproduces a model ground state to 3.9×10^-6 Ha and reaches chemical accuracy on 3d alloy fragments with 4–14× shallower circuits than unitary coupled cluster (no advantage claimed), and a tensor-network kinetic solver compresses the distribution function with exponential rank convergence (2.2×10^-10 at bond rank 16, 0.19× storage). The honest bottom line is that nothing on the design critical path waits on quantum hardware — and establishing that, with the numbers behind it, is the result. Key results (frozen anchors): iter = 1.8 ×10^18; iter = 1.6 2^n. Methods & codes: CGYRO, GENE, QAOA, VQE, ADAPT-VQE. Live verification: 11 gate validator(s) with live-recompute cards (5 reproduced, 5 estimated, 1 revised). See the Verification section and data/verification.csv. Related: Paper page · De-risking register · 3D model · Learn more about Kronos Part of the 2026 Kronos publication series; independently re-run and stamped in the Kronos de-risking register (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22645689). All numerical values are frozen design-point anchors; see the register. Public research artifact. No proprietary, financial, or supply-chain information is included.

title: Fast Compressive Embedding Transport for LLMs: Projective Sketches before AES-GCM
abstract: Overview Encrypted transport of high-dimensional LLM embeddings and activations can be bandwidth- and latency-intensive. A batch of N = 250 float32 vectors with d = 768 dimensions contains 768,000 bytes of plaintext data (≈750 KiB). After AES-256-GCM encryption, the resulting ciphertext is approximately 750 KiB. This self-contained prior-art note evaluates a simple compression-before-encryption pipeline: a D = 32 projective sketch using QR-derived orthonormal rows, followed by encryption with the same AES-256-GCM primitive and key length used for the full-dimensional baseline. Colab Benchmark Seed: 42Modeled uplink: 15 MbpsBatch: N = 250Original dimensionality: d = 768Sketch dimensionality: D = 32 Pipeline QR + Projection AES Encryption TX @ 15 Mbps AES Decryption Ciphertext Total Full 768-d — 0.366 ms 409.61 ms 0.381 ms 750.03 KiB (768,028 B) 410.36 ms Sketch D = 32 128.011 ms* 0.021 ms 17.08 ms 0.020 ms 31.28 KiB (32,028 B) 145.13 ms * The QR value represents a cold-start computation on the client CPU, timed separately from the cryptographic operations. When the projection matrix U is cached or generated deterministically from a PRNG seed, projection reduces to a comparatively inexpensive matrix multiplication. Under this recurring-use scenario, the end-to-end cost is approximately encryption + transmission + decryption ≈ 18 ms under the same 15 Mbps network model. Observed Gains Metric Improvement Ciphertext size 95.8% reduction (24× smaller) AES encryption time 17.3× faster AES decryption time 19.1× faster Transmission time 24× lower Total latency, including cold QR 2.83× lower Recurring end-to-end latency with cached projection ≈18 ms The benchmark therefore illustrates that reducing the transmitted representation from 768 to 32 dimensions can substantially reduce ciphertext size, cryptographic processing time, and network transmission latency, while retaining the same AES-256-GCM encryption primitive for both pipelines.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Transformations: A Probabilistic Modeling Approach
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-linear geometric transformations to probabilistic modeling, aiming to enhance predictive accuracy through the integration of machine learning. Traditional probabilistic models often rely on fixed parameters, while this approach leverages geometric transformations to establish a more flexible and potentially more accurate representation of underlying data relationships. The core mechanism involves constructing a probabilistic model utilizing these transformations, followed by supervised learning to refine the model's parameters. The study demonstrates a significant improvement in prediction performance compared to existing methods, highlighting the potential of this novel approach.

title: Dynamic Probability Graphs: Generation and Inference Engine
abstract: Dynamic Probability Graphs (DPG) represent a novel approach to graph-based reasoning, offering enhanced efficiency and adaptability compared to traditional methods. This paper proposes a novel generation and inference engine designed to iteratively adjust node and edge weights based on probabilistic feedback, leading to more effective decision support systems. We introduce a dynamic probability graph generation mechanism that dynamically modifies graph structure, enabling flexible system design. The core mechanism leverages the inherent probabilistic nature of the graph to optimize decision-making. This work explores the design of a robust and adaptable engine for dynamic graph manipulation, addressing limitations of existing approaches. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance in various decision-making scenarios.

title: Non-Linear Random Matrix Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on non-linear random matrices, designed to efficiently and stably search for optimal solutions in complex systems. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the matrix weights, allowing for adaptation to evolving environments. We demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of simulations and analyses, highlighting its superior performance compared to traditional methods in scenarios exhibiting dynamic changes. The core mechanism involves probabilistic weight adjustment, ensuring rapid convergence and robustness.

title: 自适应拓扑的量子计算的参数调整算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for parameter adjustment in quantum computation, leveraging the principles of adaptive topology. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on fixed algorithms, struggling to effectively handle complex environments. We propose a dynamic adjustment approach that utilizes the self-assembling process of quantum systems, dynamically modifying topological control parameters to optimize quantum computation performance and efficiency. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated optimization process guided by the inherent properties of the quantum system, ultimately leading to enhanced computational capabilities. This research explores the potential of this adaptive approach to overcome the limitations of conventional parameter tuning and advance the field of quantum computing.

title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit Compilation with Error Mitigation
abstract: Quantum circuit compilation is a fundamental step in quantum computing, translating high-level quantum algorithms into sequences of gates executable on a specific quantum hardware. However, current compilation methods often employ static decompositions, neglecting the inherent noise characteristics of quantum devices, leading to suboptimal circuit designs and reduced fidelity. This work proposes a novel adaptive quantum circuit compilation strategy that dynamically adjusts circuit decompositions in real-time, based on continuous monitoring of hardware noise profiles. The core of this approach lies in integrating quantum error mitigation techniques with a feedback loop that iteratively refines the circuit design to minimize the detrimental effects of noise. We introduce a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of this adaptive compilation process, demonstrating potential improvements in circuit fidelity and execution time. This research directly addresses the critical need for real-time adaptive compilation, a cornerstone for the practical realization of fault-tolerant quantum computing. The presented methodology offers a promising path towards more efficient and robust quantum algorithms, ultimately contributing to the advancement of quantum information processing.

title: Adaptive Differential Privacy via Dynamic Thresholding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to differential privacy, termed Adaptive Differential Privacy via Dynamic Thresholding, designed to mitigate the trade-off between privacy protection and data utility. Current differential privacy mechanisms frequently rely on fixed noise levels, which can be overly conservative, leading to significant utility loss, or insufficiently robust, failing to adequately protect against sophisticated privacy attacks. Our method addresses these limitations by dynamically adjusting the noise level applied to queries based on a learned estimation of the query's sensitivity and the current state of the data stream. This dynamic thresholding scheme, coupled with a learned sensitivity estimator, provides a more efficient and adaptive approach to privacy preservation, offering enhanced privacy guarantees while minimizing the impact on data utility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and provide a framework for its implementation. The core innovation lies in the real-time feedback loop that allows the system to respond intelligently to variations in data characteristics, representing a significant advancement over traditional static differential privacy techniques.

title: Conflict-Aware Enterprise Retrieval: Preserving Organizational Disagreement Across Heterogeneous Knowledge Sources
abstract: This preprint presents Conflict-Aware Enterprise Retrieval, a system-design framework for preserving organizational disagreement across heterogeneous enterprise knowledge sources. The approach extracts structured claims, models relationships such as SUPPORTS, CONTRADICTS, SUPERSEDES, and CHALLENGES, incorporates provenance and temporal state, and uses deterministic answerability policies to decide when an AI system should answer, warn, abstain, or block automation. The work focuses on enterprise engineering scenarios in which approved decisions, implementation state, operational evidence, documentation, and discussion may disagree. The paper proposes an evaluation methodology and benchmark design; empirical implementation results are left for future work.

title: Symbolic Logic Inference for Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program synthesis by leveraging symbolic logic inference. The core idea is that program synthesis fundamentally relies on reasoning about program behavior using logical rules. We introduce a symbolic logic-based inference engine designed to translate high-level specifications into executable code. This engine utilizes logical rules and constraints to iteratively refine and generate code that aligns with the given requirements. The key contribution lies in the application of symbolic logic, which provides a precise and verifiable framework for representing and manipulating program properties, leading to improved efficiency and accuracy compared to traditional program synthesis methods. The system constructs a logical representation of the desired program and employs inference rules to deduce the corresponding code, ensuring that the generated program satisfies the original specification. This work presents a foundational framework for symbolic program synthesis, aiming to bridge the gap between formal specification and executable code.

title: 拓扑空间数据压缩算法的量子化模拟
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum simulation techniques to data compression, specifically focusing on the unique properties of topological spaces. Traditional data compression methods often rely on classical simulation, which can be computationally expensive and limited in its ability to effectively handle the inherent structure of topological data. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum simulation to compress data by modeling the underlying quantum states of the topological space. We demonstrate the potential of this method to achieve significantly higher compression rates compared to existing techniques, leveraging the inherent properties of topology for enhanced data representation. The core mechanism involves simulating the quantum evolution of data within a topologically constructed space, leading to a compression ratio significantly improved through quantum effects. We explore the fundamental principles of quantum simulation within the context of data compression and present preliminary results showcasing the effectiveness of this methodology.

title: 基于自适应的机器学习的特征评估策略
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to feature evaluation based on adaptive machine learning. Traditional methods often rely on predefined parameter sets, struggling to effectively handle data complexity. This work proposes a self-adaptive learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts feature weights and selection, ultimately enhancing model performance. The core mechanism revolves around continuous, automated adjustments to feature representations, driven by feedback from the data itself. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of experiments across diverse datasets, illustrating its ability to outperform traditional methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

title: Information Entropy Quantum Computation
abstract: Information entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty, plays a crucial role in various fields, including data analysis, cryptography, and machine learning. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement and information entropy to develop a novel computational model. We propose a quantum entanglement-based algorithm designed to efficiently compute complex probability distributions, offering a pathway toward deeper quantum computing applications. The core mechanism centers on leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to accelerate calculations and facilitate the construction of advanced quantum machine learning models. This research investigates the feasibility of applying this approach to address challenges in traditional computational methods, specifically focusing on enhanced probabilistic computation and the exploration of novel quantum machine learning paradigms. We aim to demonstrate the potential of this approach to significantly improve computational efficiency and unlock new possibilities within quantum information processing.

title: Based on Time Window Sliding Average: A Deep Learning Model Update Approach
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to updating deep learning models, termed "Based on Time Window Sliding Average." The core idea is to mitigate the instability often encountered in traditional deep learning model updates by employing a time window sliding average technique for smoothing parameter changes. This method involves calculating a weighted average of model parameters over a defined time window. The weights typically decrease with increasing distance from the current time step, providing more influence to recent updates while still accounting for historical information. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through analysis and theoretical justification. The key contribution lies in providing a robust and stable method for updating deep learning models, particularly in environments characterized by noisy or fluctuating input data. The paper explores the impact of the window size parameter and demonstrates its influence on model performance. We argue that this simple yet effective technique can significantly improve the overall stability and convergence of deep learning models. ---

title: Context-Aware Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to program synthesis, termed "Context-Aware Program Synthesis," which leverages program execution context to generate more effective and environment-specific code. Traditional program synthesis methods often operate in isolation, neglecting the crucial influence of the runtime environment. This work addresses this limitation by incorporating a context modeling module that learns and represents the characteristics of the execution environment. The synthesized code is then guided by these contextual features, leading to improved efficiency and adaptability. The core claim is that analyzing program execution context – encompassing data dependencies, control flow, and system resources – significantly enhances the capabilities of program synthesis. This approach represents a substantial advancement in the field, moving beyond static analysis towards a more dynamic and intelligent synthesis process. The system is designed to produce code that is not only functionally correct but also optimized for the specific operational conditions.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, yet its performance often hinges on the selection of an appropriate kernel function. Traditional approaches to kernel selection are largely static, relying on predefined kernels or manual tuning, which can be inefficient and suboptimal for complex state spaces. This paper introduces an adaptive kernel learning algorithm designed to overcome these limitations. The core idea is to utilize a recurrent neural network (RNN) to dynamically learn and adjust kernel parameters based on the agent's experiences – specifically, the observed rewards and state transitions. This approach allows the agent to adapt its kernel function in real-time, leading to improved learning performance and generalization capabilities. The algorithm's key mechanism involves conditioning the RNN on the current state, reward, and action taken, effectively learning a dynamic kernel function tailored to the specific environment. We demonstrate, theoretically and conceptually, the potential of this adaptive approach to address the challenges of kernel selection in reinforcement learning.

title: 基于动态图的符号逻辑的量子计算
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of dynamic graph-based symbolic logic for enhancing quantum computation, specifically focusing on achieving more powerful logical operations and data processing capabilities. We explore how the transformation of symbolic logic into a dynamic graph framework, coupled with quantum computation's inherent randomness, can lead to significant improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy. This work aims to address key challenges in quantum computing by introducing a novel approach that leverages dynamic graph structures to facilitate complex logical operations and data manipulation. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting graph connections, and utilizing quantum randomness to implement sophisticated logical operations, ultimately pushing the boundaries of quantum algorithm design. The paper demonstrates the feasibility of this approach and highlights its potential impact on various quantum computing applications, particularly in artificial intelligence.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Neural Networks with Adversarial Temporal Regularization
abstract: Dynamic Bayesian Neural Networks (DBNNs) are a powerful framework for modeling temporal dependencies, particularly useful in scenarios where the underlying system evolves over time. However, traditional DBNNs often suffer from instability in their learned representations, leading to poor performance over extended time horizons. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing Adversarial Temporal Regularization (ATR) to DBNNs. ATR employs an adversarial network that attempts to predict future states given the current network's output. This forces the main DBNN to learn more robust and temporally coherent representations, thereby enhancing stability. We formulate the training process as a minimax game between the main DBNN and the adversary. The core claim is that standard DBNNs struggle to maintain stable representations over time, and ATR provides a novel mechanism to mitigate this issue. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ATR in improving the temporal stability and predictive accuracy of DBNNs across various benchmark tasks.

title: Syntactic Patterns and Stylistic Functions in Narrative Prose: A Rule-Based and Machine-Learning Approach
abstract: This paper presents a small-scale quantitative experiment that links syntactic structure to stylistic functions in narrative prose. Starting from a dependency-parsed corpus of 3,300 sentences, we derive sentence-level stylistic labels across five categories --- descriptive, introspective, causal, ideological, and neutral --- using a transparent rule-based procedure that inspects lemmas, universal part-of-speech tags, and syntactic relations. For each sentence we construct a compact representation of its syntactic profile as a sequence of linearised triples combining lemma, POS tag, and dependency relation. These patterns serve as input to standard machine-learning classifiers trained to predict sentence-level style. The best-performing model achieves a macro-F1 of 0.948 under 10-fold cross-validation. The experiment is implemented entirely in Python using open-source tools. Our goal is not to propose a fully fledged stylistic theory, but to offer a reproducible and extensible workflow for exploring how grammatical structure contributes to narrative interpretation.

title: DGCPath: Distribution-Aware Generative Contrastive Framework for Self-supervised Path Representation Learning -- Extended Version
abstract: Due to the proliferation of vehicle trajectory data enabled by advanced sensing technologies, path representation learning has become a pivotal task in intelligent transportation systems. Although existing self-supervised approaches have achieved promising performance, their dependence on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies inherently restricts their cross-scenario generalization capabilities. To address these limitations, we present DGCPath, an innovative Distribution-aware Generative Contrastive learning framework for Path representation. This framework establishes a synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning, enabling the acquisition of robust and transferable feature embeddings. Specifically, our framework incorporates: (1) a diffusion-based view generator that autonomously produces semantically coherent yet diverse trajectory views from Gaussian noise; (2) a variational contrastive mechanism that enforces latent feature alignment at the distribution level, transcending conventional instance-wise consistency; and (3) a novel generative cross-supervision module that reinforces view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning. Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.

title: Code and data for: Accelerating AutoML Pipeline Search through Robust Bayesian Optimization with Adaptive Acquisition Functions
abstract: This deposit contains the implementation and complete experimental results for a unified Robust Bayesian Optimization framework spanning three stages of AutoML pipeline search: data preprocessing, model selection with hyperparameter optimization, and neural architecture search. The framework uses a Gaussian Process surrogate with domain-adaptive kernels (Matérn 5/2 for continuous and categorical subspaces, a Weisfeiler-Lehman graph kernel for DAG-structured architectures) and an Expected Improvement acquisition function whose exploration weight is modulated by surrogate maturity.Contents:Python implementation of the framework and all baselines (Random Search, BO with a fixed RBF kernel)stage1_results.csv — 577 completed runs across 63 OpenML-CC18 tasks (preprocessing search)stage2_results.csv — 1,158 completed runs across 64 OpenML-CC18 tasks (model selection and HPO)stage3_results.csv — 30 completed runs on NATS-Bench TSS (neural architecture search)Each results file records per-run best accuracy, evaluations-to-95%-optimal, wall-clock time, and the full search trajectory. Benchmarks used are OpenML-CC18 and NATS-Bench TSS, both publicly available.

title: openJiuwen + DeepSeek Agent Harness: state machine, tool gateway, task-level validation, and failure recovery for LLM agents
abstract: openJiuwen + DeepSeek Agent Harness: state machine, tool gateway, task-level validation, and failure recovery for LLM agents This deposit provides a complete, reproducible Agent Harness platform that runs real LLM agents (DeepSeek-V4-Flash via a configurable DeepSeek-compatible HTTP endpoint) under strict execution control, and evaluates it head-to-head against a plain ReAct agent using the same model, tools, budgets, and tasks. What is deposited- Full source of the harness runtime (execution state machine, tool gateway with schema-constrained I/O, execution budgets, loop detection, per-call trajectories), the task-level validator and independent business Oracle scoring, three tool types (calculator, read_text_file, http_get), and six business task families.- Real-model benchmark runner with isolated per-task workspaces and three comparison arms: plain ReAct, full Harness, and a Harness-without-outer-recovery ablation.- Sealed, replayable evidence packs: per-trial execution logs, state-transition diagrams, and validation reports (468 per-trial state diagrams and validation reports inside the v2 pack), plus report documents and PDFs.- 194 offline unit/schema/evidence tests, all passing on the deposited snapshot. Evaluation design (real model, same model for both arms)- Splits: development calibration (12 tasks), confirm (36 tasks x 3 repeats), fault injection (12 tasks x 3 repeats); arms react / harness / no_recovery; 3 worker processes; max 15 inner model iterations per trial.- Results are accepted only through a strict envelope: exact RESULT contract, no malformed JSON prefixes, no duplicate keys, and error results are never counted as success.- Recoverable fault families (tool parameter error, incomplete/conflicting tool result, tool loop) plus a permanently-missing-information family where the correct behavior is a grounded refusal. Headline results (as labeled; no over-claiming)- Authority-anchor tasks: plain ReAct 3/27 vs full Harness 27/27 (+88.9 pp, 24 additional successes) — labeled AUTHORITY_ANCHOR_PROVEN.- Controlled recovery trials: 0/18 -> 18/18 recoveries — labeled CONTROLLED_RECOVERY_PROVEN.- Business benchmark, current-source run (v2, provider llmapi.paratera.com, model DeepSeek-V4-Flash, temperature=0.95, top_p=0.1, JSON response_format, 3 repeats): - Confirm set: react 86/108 (79.6%), harness 89/108 (82.4%), no_recovery 85/108 (78.7%) — harness vs react +2.8 pp. - Fault set: react 28/36 (77.8%), harness 32/36 (88.9%), no_recovery 28/36 (77.8%) — harness vs react +11.1 pp. - Development set (calibration only, not pooled into the effect estimate): all arms 10/12. - Intercepted false successes (strict envelope): react 22 (confirm) + 6 (fault); harness 0. Correct refusals 8-18 per arm per set.- Natural benign-layer comparison is honestly labeled NOT statistically proven (94.4% vs 98.9%, +4.4 pp, CI lower bound -1.1 pp, p=0.219) and is retained rather than hidden. Honesty boundaries- Business-set gains are reported descriptively; no preregistered significance threshold is claimed for them. Gains reflect complete execution, spec-compliant output, and bounded recovery rather than broadened reasoning ability.- Version 1 evidence (api.deepseek.com era) is retained as historical material; it binds to run-era source that is not in the git history, whereas the v2 evidence pack binds to the current source and passes `replay_business_pack` deep replay with zero errors on this snapshot.- The development layer is never pooled with confirm/fault statistics. Reproducibility- `python -m unittest discover -s tests` -> 194 tests pass on this snapshot.- `replay_business_pack` on the sealed v2 evidence pack returns zero errors on this snapshot (source fingerprints unchanged through HEAD 12b6380; only documentation/artifacts were added after sealing).- Plain-vs-Harness comparisons use identical model, tools, budgets, and task sets; full configuration and the formal protocol are documented in the repository. License - This deposit is released under the MIT License (SPDX identifier: MIT). - The archived snapshot also carries the project's own copyright notice and third-party component statement (`LICENSE`) for attribution and dependency disclosure. The next archived version will ship the MIT license text in that file; until then, the MIT terms stated here govern this deposit as published on Zenodo. Version 1.0.0 (commit 12b6380), deposited 2026-09-07.Related: GitHub repository https://github.com/ww49t2v9h2-cpu/Huawei_programme (isSupplementTo). 中文摘要:本作品为 LLM Agent 的可靠性平台实现与评测——以同一模型(DeepSeek-V4-Flash)对普通 ReAct 与"任务验证 + 失败诊断 + 有界恢复"的 Harness 做对照。实现层证据:权威锚层 3/27 → 27/27、受控恢复 0/18 → 18/18;当前源码业务评测(v2):确认集 +2.8pp、故障集 +11.1pp(描述性口径);自然良性层如实标注未达统计显著。随附 194 项离线测试与可在当前快照上零错误深层重放的封印证据包。

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning from Operator Feedback for Fusion Control: Imitation and Policy Exploration Confined to a Control-Barrier-Certified Safe Set
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves a controller by exploring, and on a nuclear fusion plant unconstrained exploration is precisely what must never happen. We formalise and demonstrate safe reinforcement learning from operator feedback for the Kronos controller of a compact negative-triangularity spherical-tokamak breeder (design point operating limit 3.5; I_p=9.66 MA, Q=3.076, P_fus=85.04 MW, δ=-0.30, B_0=8 T, κ=2.0, R_0=1.20 m, aspect ratio A=2.5). The design separates the two questions that safe learning usually conflates. Where may the policy act? is answered once, by a control-barrier-function (CBF) certified safe set C=\x:(x) 3.5\ that no exploratory action may leave; how may it improve inside that set? is answered by learning from the operators themselves. We state the reduced plant, the safe set, the discrete-time CBF forward-invariance condition, the minimal-intervention quadratic-program (QP) safety filter, and the operator-feedback objective (behavioural cloning plus a twin-scored override reward) as explicit equations, and we cast policy admission as pre-registered inequalities. The safety guarantee is demonstrated, not asserted: over a 100-step closed-loop exploration campaign the shielded policy records zero limit crossings against 50 for the unshielded policy, holding the peak at the boundary (=3.500 versus 4.200) with the barrier value non-negative throughout (_k h=+0.000, forward invariance) and a bounded actuation u[1.061,1.250] that never reaches the available floor u_=0.5, so the certificate is not authority-limited. The learning update is disciplined by an active-learning designer whose information gain beats random selection (grounded in a 200-evaluation surrogate Bayesian-optimisation campaign that returns a calibrated confinement posterior H_98=1.007±0.030 bounding how far the policy may explore), a continual-learning scheme that shows no regression on the validated benchmark, and a gated promotion step that admits only models passing a 19/19 verification suite with automatic rollback. Beyond per-step feasibility we state a closed-loop input-to-state-stability (ISS) certificate — a learned Lyapunov function co-verified with the policy — so that the plant not only never leaves C but provably returns toward its setpoint after a disturbance; and we place the whole learned loop inside a Simplex runtime-assurance architecture in which a formally verified baseline controller reclaims authority near the boundary and an actuator-independent hardware trip forms an unconditional last line of defense, so that safety is enforced structurally, in three certified floors, and never delegated to the learner. Every quantitative claim traces to a frozen, independently reproduced anchor in the Kronos de-risking register. The result is a controller that gets better from the people who run it without ever leaving the set that is proven safe. Key results (frozen anchors): H_98 = 1.007 ±0.030; sigma = 5 %. Methods & codes: FreeGSNKE, FreeGS, CGYRO, Sauter. Live verification: 3 gate validator(s) with live-recompute cards (3 reproduced). See the Verification section and data/verification.csv. Related: Paper page · De-risking register · 3D model · Learn more about Kronos Part of the 2026 Kronos publication series; independently re-run and stamped in the Kronos de-risking register (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22645689). All numerical values are frozen design-point anchors; see the register. Public research artifact. No proprietary, financial, or supply-chain information is included.

evidence.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning from Operator Feedback for Fusion Control: Imitation and Policy Exploration Confined to a Control-Barrier-Certified Safe Set
evidence.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves a controller by exploring, and on a nuclear fusion plant unconstrained exploration is precisely what must never happen. We formalise and demonstrate safe reinforcement learning from operator feedback for the Kronos controller of a compact negative-triangularity spherical-tokamak breeder (design point operating limit 3.5; I_p=9.66 MA, Q=3.076, P_fus=85.04 MW, δ=-0.30, B_0=8 T, κ=2.0, R_0=1.20 m, aspect ratio A=2.5). The design separates the two questions that safe learning usually conflates. Where may the policy act? is answered once, by a control-barrier-function (CBF) certified safe set C=\x:(x) 3.5\ that no exploratory action may leave; how may it improve inside that set? is answered by learning from the operators themselves. We state the reduced plant, the safe set, the discrete-time CBF forward-invariance condition, the minimal-intervention quadratic-program (QP) safety filter, and the operator-feedback objective (behavioural cloning plus a twin-scored override reward) as explicit equations, and we cast policy admission as pre-registered inequalities. The safety guarantee is demonstrated, not asserted: over a 100-step closed-loop exploration campaign the shielded policy records zero limit crossings against 50 for the unshielded policy, holding the peak at the boundary (=3.500 versus 4.200) with the barrier value non-negative throughout (_k h=+0.000, forward invariance) and a bounded actuation u[1.061,1.250] that never reaches the available floor u_=0.5, so the certificate is not authority-limited. The learning update is disciplined by an active-learning designer whose information gain beats random selection (grounded in a 200-evaluation surrogate Bayesian-optimisation campaign that returns a calibrated confinement posterior H_98=1.007±0.030 bounding how far the policy may explore), a continual-learning scheme that shows no regression on the validated benchmark, and a gated promotion step that admits only models passing a 19/19 verification suite with automatic rollback. Beyond per-step feasibility we state a closed-loop input-to-state-stability (ISS) certificate — a learned Lyapunov function co-verified with the policy — so that the plant not only never leaves C but provably returns toward its setpoint after a disturbance; and we place the whole learned loop inside a Simplex runtime-assurance architecture in which a formally verified baseline controller reclaims authority near the boundary and an actuator-independent hardware trip forms an unconditional last line of defense, so that safety is enforced structurally, in three certified floors, and never delegated to the learner. Every quantitative claim traces to a frozen, independently reproduced anchor in the Kronos de-risking register. The result is a controller that gets better from the people who run it without ever leaving the set that is proven safe. Key results (frozen anchors): H_98 = 1.007 ±0.030; sigma = 5 %. Methods & codes: FreeGSNKE, FreeGS, CGYRO, Sauter. Live verification: 3 gate validator(s) with live-recompute cards (3 reproduced). See the Verification section and data/verification.csv. All numerical values are frozen design-point anchors; see the register. Public research artifact. No proprietary, financial, or supply-chain information is included.

title: Dataset for: Evaluating multimodal large language model (LLM) systems on a Transport Canada Private Pilot Licence (PPL) Exam
abstract: This dataset accompanies a study evaluating the performance of contemporary consumer-facing multimodal large language model (LLM) systems on an official Transport Canada Private Pilot Licence (PPL) sample written examination (TP 13014). Fifteen AI system configurations from OpenAI/ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and Microsoft Copilot were evaluated. Each configuration completed the same examination on three independent occasions using a standardised zero-shot prompt and a fresh chat session for each run. The models were supplied with the examination in PDF format and were required to return answers to all 100 multiple-choice questions without iterative prompting or access to the official answer key. The workbook contains the complete model responses for all three runs, the official answer key used for scoring, per-question correct/incorrect classifications, and adjusted sectional performance data. Transport Canada divides the examination into Air Law, Aeronautics, Meteorology, and Navigation sections and requires both an overall passing score and minimum performance within each section. Eleven Navigation questions depended on a Toronto VFR Navigation Chart that was referenced by the examination but was not available with the publicly accessible source material. These questions were retained in the raw response data but excluded from the primary adjusted analysis. Adjusted overall performance is therefore calculated from 89 valid questions, with the Navigation section calculated from the nine questions that could be answered using the material supplied to the models.

title: Hippocampus-Inspired Artificial Neural Network Enables Robust Classification under Sparsity: Structured versus Brute-Force Robustness
abstract: Introduction We investigate robustness to structural sparsity in a hippocampus-inspired artificial neural network (OurANN) for image classification. OurANN is composed of functional modules—dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, and CA1—rather than conventional hidden layers (see Figure 1). DG enforces sparse competitive representations, CA3 provides recurrent stabilization, CA1 integrates stabilized activity for readout, and shortcut connections (EC→CA3 and EC→CA1) preserve signal flow under sparse connectivity. Methods As a baseline, we use a conventional multilayer perceptron (CANN) with three feedforward hidden layers whose numbers of units match those of DG, CA3, and CA1. Our ANN classifier is trained using standard backpropagation (Ref. [1]), ensuring direct comparability with the CANN baseline. Using the MNIST dataset as a controlled benchmark, we sweep the inter-layer connection probability pc from 1.0 down to 0.01 and evaluate robustness using global degradation rates and robustness indices, together with local performance metrics. Results In the dense and moderate regimes (pc=1.0 ~ 0.1), OurANN and CANN exhibit nearly identical performance, indicating no intrinsic advantage under weak sparsity. Differences begin to emerge in the sparse regime (pc = 0.1 ~ 0.05), where OurANN shows slower performance degradation, in contrast to the CANN. In the extremely sparse regime (pc = 0.05 ~ 0.01), OurANN exhibits clear and persistent robustness, while CANN performance rapidly collapses. Discussion Although CANN robustness can be partially recovered through brute-force scaling of layer size, achieving robustness comparable to OurANN requires substantially increased parameter redundancy. These results distinguish structural robustness in OurANN, arising from hippocampus-inspired architectural organization, from brute-force scaling robustness in CANN, achieved through parameter expansion. Figure Figure 1: Hippocampus-inspired artificial neural network (ANN). Feedforward: EC (entorhinal cortex) → DG (dentate gyrus) → CA3 and Shortcuts (SCs): EC → CA3 and EC → CA1 and inhibitory backprojection: CA3 → DG. S: subiculum. References [1] Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., & Williams, R. J (1986) Learning representations by back-propagating errors Nature, 323, 533-536

title: 基于自适应的神经元网络架构
abstract: The design of novel neural network architectures is an ongoing area of research with significant implications for machine learning across diverse domains. This paper introduces a novel architecture, termed "Adaptive Neural Network" (ANN), which dynamically adjusts the connection weights and activation functions of neurons based on the characteristics of incoming data. This adaptive mechanism aims to improve model performance, particularly in situations involving complex data distributions. The core of this architecture is a self-tuning neural network structure, leveraging a learning and adjustment process to optimize network behavior. This approach offers a potential advantage over traditional architectures in terms of robustness and generalization, addressing a key challenge in machine learning. The paper details the design, implementation, and evaluation of the ANN, demonstrating its effectiveness through illustrative examples and quantitative analysis.

title: Quantum Entanglement Amplification and Adaptive Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, has long been a subject of intense theoretical and experimental investigation. While the phenomenon of entanglement is well-established, its potential for practical applications, particularly in computation, remains largely unexplored. This paper explores the extension of quantum entanglement to facilitate adaptive quantum computation, utilizing a novel non-local model and an optimized quantum algorithm. We argue that the introduction of non-local effects, coupled with adaptive algorithms, offers a pathway towards solving complex problems intractable with classical approaches. The core claim is that by leveraging this framework, we can achieve significant advancements in quantum computation, particularly through enhanced complexity handling.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Counterfactual Inference with Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning – the ability to reason about what *would* have happened if something had been different – is crucial for understanding complex systems, particularly multi-agent systems. However, applying counterfactual methods in this domain is significantly challenging due to the intricate interplay between agents and their environment. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging probabilistic programming to address this challenge. We propose a framework that explicitly models agent dynamics, communication, and environmental constraints within a probabilistic setting, allowing for the systematic exploration of counterfactual scenarios. The core of our approach lies in the development of a probabilistic programming language designed to facilitate the definition and execution of these scenarios. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through a theoretical analysis, highlighting its potential for uncovering causal relationships and predicting outcomes under alternative conditions. The key contributions are a formal representation of counterfactual reasoning in multi-agent systems and a practical tool for its implementation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Data Stream Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired principles to enhance anomaly detection within data streams. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on statistical models and thresholding, which can be inefficient and inaccurate when dealing with rapidly changing data streams. We propose a novel approach that leverages concepts analogous to superposition and interference, treating data stream segments as quantum states. This allows for the simultaneous exploration of multiple potential patterns and the identification of anomalies through interference effects, where deviations from expected patterns lead to a reduction in the overall probability amplitude. The core of our methodology involves constructing a quantum-inspired state representation of the stream and employing techniques resembling quantum measurement to identify deviations. We demonstrate the theoretical foundations of this approach and outline a framework for its implementation, highlighting its potential advantages over conventional methods in terms of sensitivity and efficiency. The key contribution lies in providing a tangible and computationally feasible method for integrating quantum-inspired ideas into a real-time data analysis scenario, specifically anomaly detection.

title: Formal Verification of Probabilistic Programming Languages using Markov Logic Networks
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) offer a powerful approach to modeling uncertainty and reasoning under incomplete information. However, ensuring the correctness of these programs – particularly when dealing with complex probabilistic models – remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes a novel framework for formally verifying the behavior of PPLs by leveraging Markov Logic Networks (MLNs). MLNs provide a mathematical representation of logical constraints, enabling a systematic approach to verifying program behavior under specified assumptions. The core idea is to translate a probabilistic program into an MLN representation, then utilize the MLN's inference capabilities to check if the program satisfies a given set of logical rules. We demonstrate that this approach offers a viable path toward addressing the computational intractability inherent in traditional verification techniques for probabilistic programs. The paper outlines the methodology, key concepts, and potential limitations of this approach.

title: Adaptive Nonlinear Model Parameter Optimization Framework
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive nonlinear model parameter optimization framework designed to address the challenges of optimizing complex non-linear models, particularly within the realms of machine learning and deep learning. Traditional parameter optimization methods often employ static parameter settings, hindering the ability to effectively improve model generalization and performance. Our proposed framework dynamically adjusts model parameters based on training error and gradient information, leading to a more robust and efficient optimization process. The core mechanism leverages an adaptive algorithm to continuously refine model parameters, offering a significant improvement over static optimization techniques. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework through comprehensive analysis and illustrative examples across various machine learning tasks.

title: Quantum Simulator Based on Geometric Modeling
abstract: Quantum simulation, a crucial tool for understanding complex quantum systems, has long been hampered by computational limitations. Traditional methods often struggle to accurately represent the intricate quantum behavior of large systems. This paper introduces a novel quantum simulator, Quantum Simulator Based on Geometric Modeling, which leverages the power of geometric modeling to enhance the fidelity of quantum simulations. We propose a framework where the quantum system's geometry is explicitly defined and utilized to guide the simulation process, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency, particularly for systems with intricate spatial dependencies. The core mechanism centers around meticulously constructing geometric representations of quantum systems, enabling a more precise mapping of quantum states and interactions. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods by offering a fundamentally new way to control and interpret quantum phenomena.

title: 基于多智能体协同的复杂系统建模 (Multi-Agent Collaborative Modeling of Complex Systems - MACCS)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to complex systems modeling, termed Multi-Agent Collaborative Modeling of Complex Systems (MACCS). The core claim is that effective modeling of complex systems necessitates a collaborative framework utilizing multiple intelligent agents. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a system comprised of numerous agents, each responsible for simulating a specific aspect of the complex system. These agents then interact through information sharing and decision-making processes. This approach offers a fundamentally new perspective on complex system modeling, shifting away from monolithic representations towards a distributed, agent-based methodology. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlines a potential implementation strategy, and discusses key considerations for successful MACCS deployment. Ultimately, MACCS aims to improve the accuracy, scalability, and interpretability of complex systems models.

title: Differentiable Quantum Circuit Design Language
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Differentiable Quantum Circuit Design Language (DQCDL), designed to facilitate automated quantum algorithm design through direct optimization within the circuit's parameter space. The core concept revolves around representing quantum circuits as sets of differentiable parameters and constructing a gradient model for these circuits. Utilizing optimization algorithms like gradient descent, the DQCDL enables the iterative adjustment of circuit parameters, leading to the efficient optimization of quantum algorithms. This approach contrasts with traditional manual parameter tuning methods, offering a significantly more streamlined and automated process for quantum circuit design and optimization. The paper details the language's syntax, the methodology for building the gradient model, and outlines the optimization strategies applicable within the DQCDL framework. The primary goal is to provide a framework for exploring the vast design space of quantum circuits, ultimately accelerating the development and deployment of quantum algorithms.

title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Neural Networks with Hardware-Level Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design—Dynamically Reconfigurable Neural Networks (DRNNs)—that addresses the limitations of static neural networks by incorporating hardware-level control. The core idea is to create a neural network architecture where connections between nodes can be reconfigured in real-time, adapting to fluctuating computational demands. This is achieved through a dedicated hardware system that monitors network activity and physically adjusts the connections based on learned patterns and predefined rules. The architecture utilizes a layered approach with a central control unit that manages the reconfiguration process, alongside processing nodes that execute the neural network computations. The theoretical framework outlines the key components and the mathematical models used to describe the network's behavior and the reconfiguration process. The system is designed to improve computational efficiency and responsiveness, particularly in dynamic environments. The presented approach offers a fundamentally new way to build neural networks, merging the flexibility of learning with the performance advantages of hardware-level control.

title: 基于多模态隐式语义向量的知识图谱推理
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph (KG) reasoning leveraging multi-modal implicit semantic vector representations. Traditional KG reasoning methods often rely heavily on symbolic logic, which can be computationally expensive and struggle with the complexities inherent in real-world knowledge. Our approach addresses this limitation by embedding data from various modalities – text, images, and audio – into a unified vector space. We construct a multi-modal embedding model to map these different modalities into a shared space, allowing for reasoning based on semantic similarity rather than explicit rules. The core claim of this work is that this multi-modal representation significantly improves the accuracy of KG reasoning. The key mechanism involves utilizing vector similarity measures to infer relationships between entities within the KG. This method avoids the limitations of traditional symbolic approaches by harnessing the pattern recognition capabilities of deep learning. Experimental results, although not presented in this document due to the focus on the methodology, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Quantumization of Consensus Mechanisms
abstract: This paper explores the novel concept of quantumizing classical consensus mechanisms, specifically drawing inspiration from algorithms like Paxos. The core idea revolves around encoding the state of a consensus process – such as agreement on a value – into quantum bits (qubits) and leveraging quantum entanglement for accelerated communication and voting. Traditional consensus algorithms often suffer from performance bottlenecks due to the limitations of classical communication and the inherent latency of distributed systems. By employing quantum mechanics, particularly entanglement, we propose a pathway to significantly enhance the efficiency and speed of achieving consensus. This work outlines the theoretical framework for this approach, detailing the mapping of classical states to quantum states, the utilization of entanglement for rapid information exchange, and a preliminary analysis of the potential advantages. While this research does not involve experimental validation, it lays a foundational understanding for future exploration in this burgeoning field. The primary contribution is a conceptual model that demonstrates the feasibility of translating classical consensus protocols into a quantum paradigm.

title: Modular Logic with Emergent Properties
abstract: This paper explores the potential of formalizing logic as a system of modular, interconnected sub-systems, emphasizing the emergence of behavior through interactions and constraints. We propose a novel 'modular composition' mechanism to automatically generate new modules and relationships, fostering a dynamically evolving system. Traditional approaches often struggle to adequately model emergent properties, necessitating a paradigm shift towards a system that intrinsically anticipates and responds to complex interactions. The core claim is that formalizing logic inherently supports this emergent behavior, offering a robust framework for analyzing and understanding complex systems across various domains. This work investigates the potential of this approach, demonstrating its theoretical foundations and preliminary experimental validation of its capabilities.

title: Non-Linear Topological Field Theory for Machine Learning Algorithm Integration
abstract: This paper explores the integration of non-linear topological field theory with machine learning algorithms to construct a framework capable of learning and modeling complex systems with high precision. Traditional machine learning often relies on linear models, struggling to handle complex non-linear systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages the abstract concepts of topological field theory to enhance model performance and generalization through iterative learning and optimization. This framework offers a unique pathway for addressing challenges in predictive modeling across diverse domains. The core mechanism involves the application of topological field theory-based algorithms to refine and enhance machine learning models, creating a robust and adaptable system. This research aims to provide a foundational approach for building more accurate and versatile machine learning models, particularly within systems exhibiting intricate non-linear dynamics.

title: Behind the screen: laypersons' mental models about ChatGPT
abstract: Introduction ChatGPT's conversational interface invites anthropomorphic interpretations that conflict with its underlying probabilistic architecture. Prior research has identified folk theories and conceptions of generative AI among technical laypersons, but has largely examined these mental concepts in isolation or at the group level. Less is known about how conceptualizations of ChatGPT as a deterministic, probabilistic, anthropomorphic or dynamic AI system coexist, interact, and contradict one another within technical laypersons. This study examined (RQ1) recurring qualitative mental model configurations of ChatGPT among participants and (RQ2) whether technical AI terminology was supported by mechanism-specific understanding or coexisted with misconceptions concerning the same or another functional mechanism. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with technical laypersons ( N = 21) to ask them about their understanding of how ChatGPT works. Statements were deductively coded into four mental concepts (deterministic, probabilistic, anthropomorphic, and dynamic). Mental models were constructed for each participant. Statements containing technical terminology were additionally classified according to whether the term was contradicted by the participant's explanation of the same mechanism (“Chauffeur Knowledge”) or co-occurred with a misconception in another mechanism. Results Three recurring mental model configurations emerged: (i) Predominantly Probabilistic Thinking Patterns ( n = 8); (ii) Anthropomorphic and Dynamic Thinking Patterns ( n = 4), characterized by limited probabilistic reasoning; and (iii) Predominantly Deterministic Retrieval-based Thinking Patterns ( n = 9), characterized mainly by deterministic conceptions alongside limited probabilistic awareness. All participants showed at least one misconception about ChatGPT and among 10 participants, who used technical terminology in their explanations, seven showed chauffeur knowledge, seven demonstrated correct or partially correct understanding of one mechanism alongside a misconception about another, and four participants met both criteria. Discussion Participants' mental models of ChatGPT are fragmented and often internally contradictory. Technical terminology may mask misunderstanding of the mechanism it describes or coexist with correct understanding in one domain and misconceptions in another. These findings challenge AI literacy assessments that rely predominantly on knowledge of technical terminology. Identifying recurring qualitative configurations provides a basis for developing measures that capture the complexity of mental models and may improve predictions of over-reliance on ChatGPT output.

title: Quantum Wavefunction Augmentation via Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) has emerged as a promising route for quantum-centric supercomputing, relying on classical diagonalization of the molecular Hamiltonian within a hardware-sampled determinant subspace. However, its accuracy degrades in strongly correlated regimes where the relevant determinant space exceeds what finite-shot sampling can capture. In this work, we introduce Quantum Wavefunction Augmentation via Variational Autoencoders (Q-WAVE), a hybrid method that combines determinants sampled via SqDRIFT Krylov circuits and configuration interaction singles and doubles (CISD) determinants with generative machine learning. Using a custom $β$-annealed variational autoencoder (VAE) model, Q-WAVE iteratively expands this basis toward the variational ground state. The VAE learns the wavefunction's primary support structure from the combined hardware and CISD seed in a continuous latent space, generating new dominant determinants beyond any fixed excitation hierarchy. The resulting compact wavefunction exceeds what can be extracted from raw hardware samples alone. We demonstrate sub-millihartree accuracy compared to full configuration interaction for $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{N}_2$ dissociation. Finally, we establish Q-WAVE's scalability on a 52-qubit ethylene system (achieving sub-millihartree accuracy versus CCSD(T)) and a highly correlated 60-qubit $\text{Cr}_2$ stress test that attains chemical accuracy upon a final perturbative correction.

title: Nothing Breaks: No Single Peer Can Soundly Gate Post-Quantum Delivery
abstract: Post-quantum protection is delivered to a peer, not declared in a file: whether a session is quantum-resistant is a relation between a server's configuration and the clients that reach it. We show that no single peer can soundly gate that relation. Shipped SSH clients are not ordered: two of their post-quantum capability classes are minimal and incomparable, so a check pinned to either misses the other family's withdrawal. A peer taking both fares no better: it falls back and misses both, or, where classical outranks one family, catches just that one. No case flags both. Nothing above the wire carries the relation either. An artifact-side instrument cannot encode it, because a peer population is not one of its inputs; and across seven configurations on two protocols we find that not one of the five scalars deployed auditors expose to automation moves, while unrelated degradation moves the ones that discriminate at all: the auditors do compute the delivered algorithm, and discard it at the interface automation reads. Nothing else catches the loss either, because nothing breaks: removing a hybrid key exchange starts the daemon, validates the configuration, passes the tests and serves the client, and the adversary it defends against does not exist yet, so no functional signal can carry the loss even in principle. We then show that agents make that state reachable at scale, driving a validated downgrade in 40 of 40 episodes from ordinary engineering prose, against 0 of 40 on a matched neutral document.

title: The Art of Hierarchical Competing Patterns: Gaussian Process Optimization of Hyphenation
abstract: Hyphenation patterns remain a compact and widely deployed solution for word breaking in typesetting systems, text processors, and web rendering engines, but their generation still depends on manually tuned patgen program parameter profiles. We formulate patgen profile selection as a black-box hyperparameter optimization problem and evaluate Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization for this task. The search objective combines a precision-oriented F_{1/7}-score with an explicit trie size-accuracy trade-off using a normalized trie-size penalty. We evaluate the method on 17 hyphenated word-list datasets covering 14 languages and multiple scripts. Against two strong hand-tuned profiles regenerated from the same 8/10 training split and evaluated on the same 1/10 held-out test split, the GP-optimized profiles improve F_{1/7} on 16 of 17 datasets and reduce trie size on all 17. The median optimized/baseline trie ratio is 0.407. A dataset-level sign test gives p = 1.37e-4; a separate budget-matched comparison on five representative datasets shows that systematic search is competitive and usually improves over the best hand-tuned profile under the fixed comparison objective. The results show that model-based optimization can make pattern generation more reproducible and less dependent on expert trial-and-error while keeping the accuracy-compactness trade-off explicit.

title: Beyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.

title: ADAPTIVE CONTEXT MANAGEMENT IN LONG-CONTEXT GENERATIVE AI SYSTEMS - A VALIDATION-ORIENTED FRAMEWORK
abstract: Long-context generative artificial intelligence systems are no longer isolated neural models. When used, the UIs, retrievers, vector store, memory service, tool controller, safety filter, model runtime, cache, and accelerator infrastructure together provide a response to the user. This paper depicts how adaptive context management may be formulated as a cross-layer systems problem arising from long-context large language models and retrieval-augmented generation. The paper consolidates work on Transformers, long-context evaluation, RAG, GraphRAG, KGG-RAG, agentic RAG, memory systems, MCP-style tool connectivity, guardrails, verification, efficient inference, and telecom-focused deployment. The key contribution is a five-layer Adaptive Context Management Framework comprising the application, processing, model, data-memory and infrastructure layers. According to this framework, context is a rare resource that decays over time. Context selection approaches are formulated as an optimization problem, constrained utility optimization, to optimize relevance and source authority, freshness, memory importance, token/compute cost, privacy/security risk. The paper also outlines quantifiable validation metrics such as evidence support ratio, risk of hallucination score, latency decomposition, energy proxy, and multi-objective context-policy utility. The recommended system is described as additive to Sself-RAG, GraphRAG, Agentic RAG, MCP-like device accessibility, and long context model interfaces, not alternative to those. Since no claim is made of implementation results, I will frame the contribution as a framework/blueprint of validation-oriented research. A telecom focused validation plan will be proposed using anonymized or synthetic network logs, configuration changes, vendor manuals, incident tickets, alarms, policy documents etc. The argument presented in the paper is that larger context windows and fixed top-k retrieval alone cannot solve the issues of context dilution, lost-in-the-middle, stale memory, retrieval noise, prompt injection, privacy leakage, latency growth, and energy cost.

title: GeoProofBench v0.1: a machine-checked proposition set for digital elevation model analysis
abstract: Digital elevation model (DEM) analysis underlies terrain-related work across geomorphology, hydrology, and civil engineering, yet published algorithms are rarely machine-checked. GeoProofBench (GPB) v0.1 is a proposition set of terrain-analysis claims expressed in Dafny and Lean 4, with a reproducible pipeline that compiles each proposition to a numerical witness, a Wolfram symbolic check, and a manim visualization, keyed to a GPB-N ENTRY: PASS verdict. This deposit contains six first-order operators, composition records (including fill-then-watershed), counter-example grids, five noise levels, four DEM stacks plus three public product windows (USGS 3DEP lidar, Alaska IFSAR, Copernicus GLO-30), Dafny/Lean sources, Python/Wolfram drivers, and mp4 animations. Data are licensed CC-BY-4.0; software is licensed MIT. Public file access is intended at journal acceptance; until then the record may be restricted.

title: CCC Structural Folding Runtime: Metric Clustering, Structural Merge, and Runtime Localization
abstract: CCC Structural Folding Runtime (CSFR) is a general structural runtime framework for transforming metric-space object collections into folded CCC structures that support runtime dispatch, structural localization, and localized intelligence. CSFR distinguishes object-to-object distance (D_PP), object-to-CCC distance (D_PC), and CCC-to-CCC distance (D_CC); introduces policy-compressed Cluster CCCs and aligned Sequence Claw-Dragon Merge; and extends runtime search through CCC DNA, reverse structural indexing, Two-Way CCC, and Two-Phase Structural Search. The canonical runtime progression is: Metric -> Cluster -> Merge -> CCC -> DNA -> Retrieve -> Verify -> Localization. The repository also includes Stock-Market Structural Folding as the first canonical application case, demonstrating how historical metric-space patterns can be folded into runtime-localizable structural regimes while keeping structural localization distinct from downstream prediction.

title: High-Dimensional Space Distribution Probability Modeling Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of machine learning to optimize probability models for high-dimensional space distributions. Traditional approaches often rely on manual parameter tuning, presenting challenges in terms of computational cost and model robustness. We propose a novel model that leverages machine learning to automatically adjust model parameters, resulting in improved predictive accuracy. The core mechanism centers around establishing a probabilistic model for high-dimensional space distributions, utilizing machine learning to iteratively refine the model's parameters to enhance accuracy. This research addresses a key need in probabilistic modeling, offering a more efficient and adaptable approach compared to traditional methods. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the model's performance, highlighting the benefits of automated parameter optimization.

title: Non-Euclidean Geometry and Quantum Entanglement Models
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-Euclidean geometry to quantum entanglement, proposing a novel model that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to create novel computational paradigms. The core mechanism centers on the design of a non-Euclidean geometric framework rooted in quantum entanglement, investigating its potential within quantum information processing and quantum algorithm development. We aim to demonstrate how this model can provide a new perspective on geometric principles and potentially unlock advanced computational capabilities. This work investigates the implications of exploring the interplay between geometric intuition and quantum entanglement.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Constraint Networks for Adaptive Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the application of self-organizing constraint networks (SOCN) to adaptive evolutionary algorithms, aiming to improve the robustness and efficiency of optimization processes. SOCN leverages the inherent adaptability of constraint networks, combined with feedback loops, to dynamically adjust constraint parameters during the evolution of a solution. The core mechanism centers around nodes that iteratively adjust their constraints based on the algorithm's performance, fostering a self-optimizing structure that mitigates local optima and explores the solution space more effectively. We propose a framework that allows the network to learn and adapt its constraints, leading to improved convergence and solution quality. This work contributes to the development of more effective evolutionary algorithms capable of handling complex, dynamic problem spaces.

title: Title: Adaptive Probability Space Construction
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Probability Space Construction, a novel method for building probabilistic space. The core principle centers around iteratively constructing a 'probability landscape' through reinforcement learning, meticulously balancing the model's inherent randomness with predictive power. The method leverages a 'Probabilistic Landscape Generator' that utilizes reinforcement learning to construct a network of probabilities, ensuring a dynamic and adaptable system. This approach aims to address limitations in traditional probabilistic modeling by providing a framework for inherent randomness and predictive performance. The concept is predicated on the idea of learning a 'landscape' of probabilities, where each point represents a possible outcome and the system learns to navigate and exploit these landscapes to maximize predictive accuracy. We present a theoretical framework outlining the key components and potential challenges of this method, demonstrating its adaptability through illustrative examples.
